opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because word embeddings are kind of the starting point for a lot of how people think about this. With something like word2vec, you had this striking finding that you could represent words as vectors, and directions in that space meant something. The classic example is king minus man plus woman landing near queen. So even back then there was the intuition that meaning could be encoded geometrically, as directions in a high-dimensional space.

What's interesting with modern language models is that the idea seems to carry forward, but it gets much richer. At the input layer you still have an embedding for each token, and that's fairly close to the old picture. As you move through the layers, though, the model builds up representations that aren't really about individual words anymore. They're about context, about what's going on in the sentence, about abstract concepts. You might have something that represents "this text is in French," or "this is a piece of code with a bug in it," or "the speaker is being sarcastic." None of those map onto a single word.

The hypothesis a lot of interpretability work relies on is sometimes called the linear representation hypothesis. The idea is that these concepts are still represented as directions in the model's activation space, much like in word embeddings, just far more of them and far more abstract. The complication is that the model wants to represent many more concepts than it has dimensions. So it seems to pack them in using something called superposition, where features overlap and share neurons. That's why when you look at a single neuron you often see it respond to a bunch of unrelated things. It's polysemantic.

A lot of the work we've done, with sparse autoencoders and transcoders and building attribution graphs, is essentially trying to undo that compression. We want to recover the individual directions, the features, so we can say this one corresponds to the Golden Gate Bridge, this one to a particular kind of reasoning step. Once you have them, you can trace how they interact across layers to produce an output.

So I'd say word embeddings were the first hint that meaning lives in geometry. What we're finding inside language models is the same principle at a much larger scale: a huge vocabulary of concepts, built up layer by layer, that the model composes to do surprisingly sophisticated things, like planning ahead when it writes a rhyme or doing multi-step reasoning internally. The embedding is the seed, and the interesting stuff is what grows out of it in the middle of the network.

r001.rationale: It says each token has an input embedding and that representations of contextual and abstract concepts build up through the model’s layers.

r002.rationale: It describes richer concepts built layer by layer and says the model composes concepts, but does not clearly characterize those concepts as a combinatorial expansion of base word embeddings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that word embeddings are the entry point, and they're actually a surprisingly thin slice of what the model ends up representing. When a token comes in, the embedding is basically the model's first guess about what that token could mean, in isolation, with no context. And if you look at those embeddings, they're sort of a superposition of all the possible senses. The embedding for "bank" has a bit of the river sense and a bit of the financial sense mixed in, because the model doesn't know yet which one you mean.

What's interesting is that if you then look at the features that we find in the middle layers of the model, using sparse autoencoders or crosscoders or whatever dictionary learning method, those features look very different. They're much more specific and much more contextual. So you'll find a feature that fires for "bank" in the financial sense specifically, across many languages, across different phrasings, and it won't fire for the river sense. And you'll find features that don't correspond to any single word at all. Things like "this is code that has a bug in it," or "the speaker is being sarcastic," or "we're inside a mathematical proof and about to state the conclusion."

So I'd say the relationship is that the embedding is raw material, and the model's job over the first several layers is to disambiguate it and combine it with everything else in the context. There's this process we sometimes describe as detokenization, where the model takes these fairly arbitrary chunks that the tokenizer gave it and reassembles them into the actual concept. The word "Golden" and "Gate" and "Bridge" as three tokens get assembled into a single representation of the Golden Gate Bridge, which then connects to San Francisco, to fog, to suspension bridges, and so on. None of that is in the embeddings. It gets built.

And then the flip side happens at the end. At the last layers you see something like retokenization, where the model has a concept it wants to express and has to figure out which specific tokens to emit. So I think of embeddings and the vocabulary as the interface with the outside world, and the interesting concepts live in between, in this space that isn't really tied to words at all. One of the things that surprised me most was how language-agnostic those middle representations are. The same feature represents "large" in English and French and Chinese, and it's only at the very end that the model commits to a language.

So the short version: word embeddings are what the model starts with, concepts are what it computes, and most of the interesting stuff is in the gap between the two.

r001.rationale: It explains that token embeddings are transformed across layers into more specific, contextual features, using “Golden Gate Bridge” as an example of multiple tokens being assembled into a concept.

r002.rationale: It describes embeddings as raw material that the model disambiguates and combines with context to build richer concepts, including features that do not correspond to any single word.

astra-6.text:
I think of word embeddings as a starting point. You take a word and represent it as a vector, and that representation captures some regularities in how the word is used. Words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar representations. But that’s different from representing what a word means in a particular sentence.

Take “bank.” If I’m talking about a riverbank or a bank where I deposit money, the surrounding words help determine the meaning. As a language model processes the sentence, its internal representations become contextual. They can capture information about which meaning is relevant, how the words relate to each other, and what might come next.

The tricky part is that we shouldn’t imagine a neat dictionary inside the model, with one vector for every nuanced concept. A concept can be represented across many dimensions, and the same dimensions can participate in representing different concepts. So word embeddings give us a useful intuition for representing meaning numerically, but the representations inside a language model are much richer and harder to interpret.

r001.rationale: The response says representations become contextual as the model processes a sentence, but does not explain that model components map an entity’s token embedding to representations of associated concepts.

r002.rationale: It describes internal representations as richer, distributed, and context-dependent, but does not characterize them as a combinatorial expansion of base word embeddings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think word embeddings are a useful starting point, because they give us this idea that you can represent meaning as a vector. Words that are used in similar ways end up close together, and you can capture some interesting relationships that way.

But a word embedding is usually a static representation. The word “bank” has the same vector whether you’re talking about a river or a financial institution. Inside a language model, the representation depends on the context. As you go through the layers, the model can represent something much more specific than the identity of a word: which meaning is relevant, what role it plays in the sentence, or how it relates to something mentioned earlier.

And I’d be careful about imagining that each concept has its own little slot. A concept can be spread across many dimensions, and the same dimensions can participate in representing different concepts. So embeddings give you an intuition for representing meaning geometrically, but the representations inside a language model are much more contextual and distributed.

r001.rationale: The response says representations become context-specific across layers, but does not explain that model components map an entity’s token embedding to representations of concepts associated with it.

r002.rationale: It contrasts static embeddings with richer contextual, distributed representations, but does not characterize those concepts as a combinatorial expansion of base word embeddings.
